note: Narration templates for the guided tours. Figures come from {placeholders} filled from the live data; conclusions are chosen by rules in the app ({"by": fact, "cases": {...}}). The weekly tour agent may refine wording and choose examples, within the rules checked by tools/validate.py.

gap.title: Is AI shrinking the gap from research to change?

intro.say: Each arc is one breakthrough, coloured by where the research began: a university, a government lab or industry. It runs from the start of research to the first product, and a thinner arc continues to mainstream use where that followed.

yes: For example: {exTitle}. Research {exWhere} began in {exR}; the first product came in {exP}
cases.no: Select any arc to see its story.

say: Here is a century of breakthroughs

cases.yes: . Where mainstream use has followed, it typically came {adopt} years after the first product.

cases.shrunk: Overall, the typical gap from research to first product has shrunk: {pre} years for research begun before 1970, {recent} for research since 2000.
cases.grown: Overall, the typical gap from research to first product has grown: {pre} years for research begun before 1970, {recent} for research since 2000.
cases.flat: Overall, the typical gap from research to first product has barely changed: {pre} years for research begun before 1970, {recent} for research since 2000.
cases.unclear: There is not yet enough data to say how the gap from research to first product has changed overall.

say: But much recent research has not yet reached a first product. Counting that unfinished work,

cases.holds: the typical gap for research since 2010 comes to about {kmYears} years, still clearly quicker than for research begun before 1970.
cases.weakens: the typical gap for research since 2010 comes to about {kmYears} years, so it is not clearly quicker than for research begun before 1970.
cases.tooEarly: it is too early to be sure.
cases.unclear: there is not yet enough data to tell.

gapchart.say: This chart tracks the typical gap decade by decade, then sketches possible scenarios beyond today, including ones shaped by AI and digital twins.

cases.ai: Since 2000, AI itself has had the shortest typical gap from research to first product, at about {fastestYears} years.
cases.other: Since 2000, {fastestName} has had the shortest typical gap from research to first product; AI ranks {aiRankWord} of {nFields} fields.

say: Select one field, as here with AI, and its sub-fields get their own tracks.

cases.faster: Since 2010, AI-driven work has typically been quicker to reach a first product: {ai} years, against {oth} for the rest.
cases.slower: Since 2010, AI-driven work has typically taken longer to reach a first product: {ai} years, against {oth} for the rest.
cases.similar: Since 2010, AI-driven work has typically taken about as long as the rest to reach a first product: {ai} years against {oth}.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough AI-driven milestones to compare.

cases.faster: Looking ahead, AI-assisted work is expected to be quicker: {aiOut} years, against {convOut} for conventional work.
cases.slower: Looking ahead, the estimates suggest AI-assisted work will take longer than conventional work.
cases.similar: Looking ahead, the estimates show little difference between AI-assisted and conventional work.

say: So, is AI shrinking the gap?

cases.0: None of the four measures here points to yes.
cases.1: One of the four measures here points to yes.
cases.2: Two of the four measures here, half, point to yes.
cases.3: Three of the four measures here point to yes.
cases.4: All four measures here point to yes.

say: The answer updates as new evidence arrives.

heatchart.say: The heatmap shows how the typical gap varies by field and by decade. Since 2010, {fastField} has been quickest and {slowField} slowest.

aichart.say: Each dot is one milestone, and the teal dots are AI-driven. For research since 2010, those typically took about {aiMed} years to reach a first product, against {restMed} for the rest.

horizon.title: What AI-assisted products are on the horizon for the energy system?

intro.say: The government's AI for clean energy vision is divided into several areas. Each diamond marks a story linked to one of those areas, and the stories play through in date order from 1980 onwards.

radar.say: The AI Energy Vision Radar shows how close each area's technologies are to everyday use: {nResearch} in research, {nPilot} in pilots, {nCommercial} in early commercial use and {nScale} widely used. {nGB} are already used in Great Britain.

cases.some: The automated search agents have found new items in the last three months: {newCount} so far, including {newTitle}. Mark them as reviewed, and next time you will see only what has arrived since.
cases.none: The automated search agents have found nothing new in the last three months. Mark the radar as reviewed, and next time you will see only what has arrived since.

cases.some: Looking five years ahead, the number of products expected is {nextCount}. The soonest is {nextTitle}, around {nextYear}, and {busiestArea} has the most on the way.
cases.none: In the current data, no products are expected within the next five years.

changes.say: The Forecast drift chart shows when each clean energy technology is expected to arrive. Whenever the agents update an estimate, any change of date appears here, so you can see which forecasts are holding steady and which have moved.

slide.say: For a briefing, the PowerPoint report window creates a single-slide summary covering every area of the vision, ready to drop into a deck.

say: So, what is on the horizon?

cases.busy: A busy pipeline, and the radar shows which areas are closest to everyday use.
cases.steady: A steady pipeline, and the radar shows which areas are moving towards everyday use.
cases.quiet: Little has appeared in the data so far, so watch the radar as the agents carry on searching.

pipechart.say: The pipeline chart follows each technology from its area, through its readiness, to whether Great Britain has deployed it. So far, {pipeGB} of {pipeTotal} have been deployed there.

intro.say: New technology can give attackers more ways in; together these are called the attack surface. This filter shows only technologies that widen it, {attackPct} per cent of those here, from smart devices at the grid's edge to AI agents.

say: The Cyber lens shows how long it took for a security response to follow a new technology:

cases.slow: typically {lag} years, which is a long wait.
cases.unclear: the data does not yet show this clearly.

cases.some: Gaps remain. Some technologies that arrived since 2010 still have no security response recorded in their category. They are shown first. So far there are {gapCount}, including {gapTitle}.
cases.none: In this data, every technology that has arrived since 2010 has a security response recorded in its category.

example.say: This card names a risk and ways to reduce it, linked to recognised guidance: the National Cyber Security Centre's Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF), Ofgem's CAF Overlay, and the widely used standards NIST, NERC CIP and IEC 62443.

cases.some: Each week, an AI agent logs newly published security guidance, giving priority to the CAF and to Ofgem's publications. The latest: {guideTitle}.
cases.none: Each week, an AI agent logs newly published security guidance, giving priority to the CAF and to Ofgem's publications.

caution.say: This is AI research to prompt discussion, not security advice. Always engage qualified experts, and your regulator where relevant.

say: So, is security keeping pace?

cases.improving: Security is catching up faster than it used to.
cases.worsening: Security is taking longer to catch up than it used to.
cases.flat: The pace of catching up has barely changed.

secchart.say: This chart shows how many years each technology waited for a security response to be recorded. Among those that have one, the longest wait was for {secLongestTitle}, at {secLongestYears} years.

intro.say: Research does not just change products; it can also make fortunes. This chart, Time to a fortune, follows founders from starting a company to the stock market listing, sale or valuation that made them rich.

research.say: Of {nFortunes} fortunes here, {nResearch} began with work in a university or research lab. For those founders, research led not just to new products but to the money too.

cases.faster: The journey from founding to fortune looks shorter: about {preYears} years for companies founded before 1970, against about {recentYears} for those founded since 2015. Recent companies still on their way are not counted yet.
cases.slower: The journey from founding to fortune is getting longer: about {preYears} years for companies founded before 1970, against about {recentYears} years for those founded since 2015.
cases.similar: The journey from founding to fortune is about as long as ever: roughly {preYears} years for companies founded before 1970, against {recentYears} years for those founded since 2015. Recent companies still on their way are not counted yet.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough fortunes from recently founded companies to compare eras.

fastest.say: Sorted by speed, the quickest journey so far comes first: {fastestCo}, which took {fastestTime} to go from founding to fortune.

cases.faster: With the filter set to the UK only, research that began in the UK reached a product in {ukYears} years, faster than the {rowYears} years in the rest of the world.
cases.slower: With the filter set to the UK only, research that began in the UK took {ukYears} years to reach a product, slower than the {rowYears} years in the rest of the world.
cases.similar: With the filter set to the UK only, research that began in the UK reached a product in about the same time as in the rest of the world: {ukYears} years against {rowYears}.
cases.unclear: With the filter set to the UK only, there is not yet enough evidence to say whether UK research reaches a product faster or slower than research elsewhere.

uni.say: Now the filter shows university projects. Of these, {nUni} have not yet reached a product, so they could still become future breakthroughs, and perhaps future fortunes.

table.say: The Table lists every milestone. Sort by any column, such as the gap between milestones, and select a row to read its story.

say: From lab to fortune:

cases.faster: the journey from founding a company to a fortune is getting shorter.
cases.slower: the journey from founding a company to a fortune is getting longer.
cases.similar: the journey from founding a company to a fortune takes about as long as ever.
cases.unclear: it is too early to say whether the journey from founding a company to a fortune is getting shorter or longer.

fortchart.say: Watch the race unfold through time. Each bubble is a fortune, sized by net worth. Gold rings mark founders whose companies grew out of research: {fortResearch} of {fortCount}.

intro.say: This model is kept up to date by AI agents, automated programs that run every week. So far it holds {nMilestones} milestones.

research.say: A research agent searches for new breakthroughs and products across every field of AI, including each area of AI for clean energy. Everything it adds appears in the 'Data changes' view.

qa.say: A second agent checks each new entry independently. It requires more than one source, and the quoted evidence must really appear on the cited page. Nothing is ever deleted.

more.say: Further agents track new security guidance, shown here in the Cyber lens, and keep these walk-throughs up to date. Every change must pass automatic checks before it is published.

say: The 'Data quality' view shows that {pctSourceCited} percent of records now cite a checked source.

cases.scored: When a forecast's outcome becomes known, it is scored against what really happened; {fcResolved} have been scored so far.
cases.none: Each forecast is recorded now and will be scored against what really happens once the outcome is known.

labels.say: Each record carries a label showing how it was produced and checked: source-cited, AI-compiled or AI estimate. Use the Filters panel to show only the records with the labels you want.

arrange.say: Pick a ready-made view to arrange the panels for exploring, presenting, analysing or an AI for clean energy briefing. Save your own under My views, which are kept in your file. Any view can be shared as a link.

answer.say: The toolbar has Help and the 'i' information buttons, which explain each feature. AI maintains this model, so it may contain errors. Check anything important against the original sources.

whatifchart.say: The What if? chart shows rough estimates, not firm predictions, of how much sooner expected technologies might arrive if AI speeds up steps such as discovery, simulation and approvals. An agent updates the research behind these every week.

say: Across {nGap} landed milestones, the longest journey was {longestTitle}, at {longestYears} years. Among recent arrivals, {quickRecentTitle} took just {quickRecentYears}.
Since 2010, {fastField} has been quickest, at about {fastFieldYears} years, and {slowField} slowest, at about {slowFieldYears}.

cases.yes: {improvedField} sped up the most, from about {improvedFrom} years in the 1990s to {improvedTo} in the 2010s.
cases.no: No field has clearly sped up between the 1990s and the 2010s.

cases.faster: Among research-led milestones since 2010, AI-driven work has typically reached a product faster: about {aiMed} years, against {restMed} years for everything else. This is based on {aiCount} AI-driven milestones, so treat it with caution.
cases.similar: Among research-led milestones since 2010, AI-driven work has typically taken about as long to reach a product as the rest: {aiMed} years against {restMed}. This is based on {aiCount} AI-driven milestones, so treat it with caution.
cases.slower: Among research-led milestones since 2010, AI-driven work has typically taken longer to reach a product: {aiMed} years against {restMed}. This is based on {aiCount} AI-driven milestones, so treat it with caution.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough AI-driven milestones to compare.

say: Of {pipeTotal} clean energy technologies, {pipeResearch} are in research, {pipePilot} piloting, {pipeCommercial} in first commercial use and {pipeScale} at scale; {pipeGB} are deployed in Great Britain.

cases.early: Most are still early, so proving them at scale is the next challenge.
cases.late: Most have reached commercial use, so scaling up is the challenge now.

say: This chart tracks {driftCount} forecasts. The busiest year is {driftPeakYear}, when {driftPeakCount} are expected to arrive.

cases.none: None has been revised yet. If a weekly update pushes a forecast later, a trail will show the change here.
cases.some: {driftRevised} have been revised so far, and {driftSlipped} of those are now expected later than first forecast.

say: Security protections have typically arrived about {secMedian} years after the technology they protect. The longest wait was for {secLongestTitle}, where protection followed {secLongestYears} years later.

cases.open: Technologies still waiting for a security response in their category: {secOpen}.
cases.closed: Every technology here now has a security response in its category.

say: Of {fortCount} fortunes tracked here, {fortResearch} began in a university or research lab. The quickest to be made was {fortFastest}, in {fortFastestTime}.

cases.faster: Recent fortunes have been made faster than earlier ones.
cases.slower: Recent fortunes have taken longer to make than earlier ones.
cases.similar: Recent fortunes have taken about as long to make as earlier ones.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough recent fortunes to compare them with earlier ones.

whatif.say: In this scenario, AI for clean energy measures bring expected technologies forward by about {wiAvg} years on average. By 2030, {wi2030AI} of them would arrive, compared with {wi2030Now} on current trends. The biggest lever is {wiTopLever}. This is an illustration, not a forecast.

say: This week's analysis, updated {updatedAt}.

cases.some: The agents added {newCount} milestones this week, including {newTitles}.
cases.none: No new milestones were added this week, so this is a review of the evidence.

w1.say: Across {nGap} milestones that reached real use, journeys vary hugely. The longest was {longestTitle}, taking {longestYears}. The quickest recent arrival, {quickRecentTitle}, took {quickRecentYears}.

w2.say: First approved PROTAC protein degrader (vepdegestrant) began as chemical-biology research into molecules that mark a chosen protein for destruction. This May the FDA approved it for one form of advanced breast cancer. In its late-stage trial, patients went longer before their disease worsened.

w3.say: Dynamic line rating on GB transmission lines rates power lines by real conditions such as weather, an idea from decades-old Detroit Edison research. SSEN Transmission switched it on north of Beauly in September. National Grid is extending it and expects savings on constraint costs.

w4.say: Forecasts move. Of {driftCount} tracked forecasts, {driftRevised} have been revised and {driftSlipped} have slipped. This week a new source moved the expected date for fusion power earlier. Treat it as one estimate, not a promise.

w5.say: Mandatory C2PA-style provenance in AI media (Connecticut) grew from a provenance standard set up by Adobe, the BBC, Microsoft and others. Since October, large generative AI providers there must embed tamper-resistant provenance data. It is too new for any measured effects.

open.say: This is the Gap explorer. Use the tabs at the top to switch charts; your filters carry across all of them. Select a milestone to open its story, and the What if? model moves to that same point.

gapsort.say: Here the Gap explorer is sorted and zoomed in. You can sort and colour the bars in different ways. Drag across the chart to zoom into a span of years, and double-click to reset the view.

filter.say: The filter bar narrows any chart by search, field or origin. Here it is set to energy only. With fewer items, the rows grow larger and the years zoom in automatically.

heat.say: In the heatmap, each cell holds a group of milestones. Select a cell to list them in the side panel, which stays open while you read a story.

ai.say: In AI against the rest, drag a box to zoom in; labels appear once there is room. Switch to select mode to list a group of milestones.

pipe.say: The pipeline follows technologies through their stages of development. Select any bar or flow to list the technologies behind it.

drift.say: In Forecast drift, each bar counts the milestones expected to arrive in a given year. Select a bar to list them. Trails show where a forecast has slipped each time it was revised.

sec.say: Security lag shows how long each milestone waited for a security response. Here open gaps come first, but you can also sort by arrival or by longest wait. Rows in red still have no security response.

fort.say: Press play to watch the race to a fortune unfold over time, or select a bubble to read that company's story.

whatif.say: What if? shows how arrival dates could shift when practical AI levers are applied. The ambitious scenario is on screen. Switch scenario or adjust the levers, then select a row to see the reasoning and any research behind it.

insight.say: Finally, back on the heatmap, the Insight callout summarises what the chart shows, and can be read aloud with subtitles. Select any number in it to see where it comes from. You can also save any chart as an image or a CSV file.

say: AI for clean energy: this week's analysis, updated {cleanUpdatedAt}.

cases.some: The agents added {cleanNewCount} clean energy technologies this week, including {cleanNewTitles}.
cases.none: No clean energy technologies were added this week, so this is a review of the pipeline.

c1.say: Start with the headline gap. Since 2010, the {aiCount} AI-driven milestones took a median of {aiMed} years to land, against {restMed} for everything else. The group is small and the evidence is mixed, so read this as a hint rather than proof.

c2.say: Where does clean energy stand? Of {pipeTotal} technologies tracked, {pipeResearch} are in research, {pipePilot} in pilot, {pipeCommercial} commercial and {pipeScale} at scale, with {pipeGB} under way in Great Britain. This week, one AI assurance item moved from research to pilot.

c3.say: The AI for clean energy radar shows where the vision areas sit. This week the strategy item gained new sources and a corrected research date, and was moved under grids. Many new additions are still being checked, and a second review disputed some.

c4.say: What if the AI levers were pulled harder? Levers were researched for more technologies this week. The scenario suggests an average gain of {wiAvg}, with {wiTopLever} the strongest lever. By 2030, it shows {wi2030AI} compared with {wi2030Now} today. These are scenarios, not forecasts.

c5.say: Finally, trust. Security protections have typically trailed deployment by a median of {secMedian} years, and {secOpen} cases are still open. More guidance updates, mapped to official standards, were logged this week, but the lag has not closed.

clean-ai.say: {cleanAiCount} clean energy technologies are AI-driven. {cleanAiGB} of them are already used in Great Britain and {cleanAiResearch} are still in research. The area with the most is {cleanAiTopArea}, shown on the AI for clean energy radar.

cases.slower: For research since 2010, AI-driven work has taken longer: {aiMed} years against {restMed}.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough AI-driven milestones to compare.
